en: Śrī, who acts in accordance with all scriptures, whose form is fashioned according to her will, and who is separated from Kandarpa by the multitude of yakṣas, [is captured] by the sage’s restraint of the arrow-like glances of the maiden.
May it bring about the accomplishment of all goals for you.
She whose nature is agitated by the *kula-kalā* (the power of the lineage), moving with beautiful grace within the sphere of the dissolution of the office of enjoyment (*bhoga-adhikāra-laya*).
I bow to her who illuminates all, blazing with the radiant splendor of sublime wisdom, and who generates the light of primordial knowledge for all worlds.
Having observed the diversity of inclinations among people, the Buddhas [taught] in the *Śrīsaṃvara* and other tantras that for boys and girls,
there is worship, as well as the attainment of results through auspicious and inauspicious signs.
Having been described here, I shall now write it down, having extracted it from that source.
If one’s mind desires to attain all supernatural powers (siddhis) residing in her sprout-like hands,
she should be worshipped according to the prescribed rite on either the eighth or the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
On a day appropriate for the rite, on the highly auspicious tenth lunar day.
For pacification (śānti), she is a daughter of a Brahmin with a white body, adorned with white garments;
for nourishment (puṣṭi), she is born of a Kṣatriya, resembling gold and adorned with yellow robes;
for subjugation (vaśya), she is born of a Vaiśya or a Śūdra artisan or dancer, red in color and wearing red garments.
In enmity, she has a son born of an internal Śūdra mixture; she is dark-complexioned and wears blue garments.
Born from various lineages, she is complete, radiant with the garments of thought,
adorned with ornaments, possessing a beautiful mind and face, and engaged in all types of ritual action; in her food, she shines in variegated raiment.
From five years onwards, and during the interval until the appearance of menses, she is "maiden" (kaumārī) for one hundred [years]; then, according to the gods, she consists of the form of a woman.
In gardens, cow-pens, roads, ports, boundaries, temples, pavilions for noble men, houses, hermitages, palaces, and so forth—
[adorned] with golden staffs, white chowries, and cymbals—
With various silken cloths hanging down like a moon-shaped parasol.
On a spot of ground made fragrant by smeared cow-dung, upon a seat of soft grass and strewn flowers, marked with beautiful signs for the great festival and perfumed with excellent incense;
Having concealed [the teaching] and having diligently removed base people.
Having invited them according to the rite for offering bath-water,
and having subsequently brought their pair of feet with due respect,
the patron of the gift should wash them and honor them in sequence with the *arghya* offering.
Facing the east or other directions, according to the prescribed method of performance.
Up to one hundred and eight, in odd numbers, or according to the sequence of the count of one's own maṇḍala,
[one should worship] upon the seat of the syllable Oṃ, on a vajra, or on a lotus.
Having established them, they were consumed and composed.
The mantra-practitioners, purified by the yoga of the *Śrīsaṃvara* and other tantras,
[visualize] young maidens born from seed-syllables radiating with the flames of gnosis,
their beautiful bodies possessing the colors and forms of the assembly of deities such as Vajraṅgaṇā.
Having purified the three bodies and so forth with one's own mantras through the intellect.
Having examined the hands, feet, and pair of cheeks with care, and having fashioned them into the form of flower garlands, ornaments, and garments,
[he adorned them] with vermilion, collyrium, kucandana, saffron, and other substances.
By the giving of the sacred thread, clothing, and ornaments.
With Aśoka, Mandāra, Turaṅgamāra, Taraṅga, Bandhūka, Kuruṇḍaka, and Arka;
with Palāśa, Bhīru, Draka, Curjila, and Lālā—
With the young shoots of the śirīṣa, ṭāḍimba, and kiṃśuka trees, and so forth.
With fragrant flowers grown on land, such as *sakunda*, jasmine, and *mallikā*,
and with water-blooming *kumuda* and *ambujanman* lotuses;
With varieties of thousand-petaled blue lotuses.
Outside the worship pavilion, people stood performing dances and playing musical instruments—
the *ḍhakkā*, *dundubhi*, *jhallarī*, and *ḍamaruka* drums— chanting hymns of great auspiciousness,
and making sounds with the *vīṇā*, flute, mṛdaṅga, and *vallarī* lutes, accompanied by the songs of those wearing anklets.
The excellent assembly of beautiful Jina-consorts was delighted by his profound and steady voices.

With various kinds of milk from the madana tree mixed with the five nectars, with abundant servings of sacrificial porridge and attendants, with varieties of fish and meat, with bowls and cups of soup, and with side dishes of jambu-fruit and dīka;
With curd, ghee, honey, *sihlā*, *phāṇita*, sweetmeats (*laḍḍuka*), and so forth. || O ||
With an unwearied mind,

while muttering the mantra, he should attentively observe through the facial expressions of the young maidens all the signs of their auspicious and inauspicious nature, as well as their gestures, voices, and dispositions.
At the time of obtaining the pleasure of enjoying offerings of food and drink.
If she suddenly wrings her hands in great anger,
proclaiming her misery as the affliction of disease increases;
or if Sundarikā then vomits, O Hero—
This is the sign of the arrival of disease among the people who perform sacrifices.
He finds no satisfaction from drinking the abundant juices of much wine; the donor will suffer the affliction of a great and terrible disease.
If he releases a most fierce cry while being exhilarated, [the same result follows].
For it does not indicate that which is to be proven here with any greater degree of certainty.
Rubbing both her eyes, the goddess cries out; it is no wonder that the giver [of gifts] may meet death in an instant.
Rubbing her feet and gazing at the sky with tearful eyes—
It is the cause of the destruction of one's mother, father, virtuous people, and the elderly.
Looking back at her back and scratching her face with her nails,
she should give [the food], thinking, "She is not satisfied by meat and such.
She watches for food to be eaten from another vessel.
That satisfaction which one feels when touching one's own belly would not be mine.
Looking at one another face-to-face, a mutual quarrel between the giver and the receiver is indicated here;
she causes them to be intensely possessed by each other, both self and other.
"A battle will take place, and it shall bring about the Kali age."
She is not satisfied by eating various kinds of food in great quantities;
moreover, diseases and other ailments suddenly arise, as does misfortune from weapons.
She repeatedly performs singing, instrumental music, and laughter;
there will be fear arising from kings, thieves, and fire.
Extremely enraged, she rubs her foot upon the surface of the ground.
The cause for the destruction of one who possesses wealth and strength in a secure location.
Having set aside all varieties of food, one should eat while keeping the host of deities desired in that place pleased;
and by avoiding idle chatter, one should suppress the telling of internal stories.
Completeness does not belong to the activity of primordial nature.
If a maiden, having looked back from the house, goes away,
there will again be an increase in the afflictions of karma for the people here; thus he discerned that inauspicious omen as a sign of transformation.
Therefore, one should perform virtuous deeds here with a concentrated mind. || O ||
Having satisfied the host of goddesses according to the ritual preceded by the ringing of bells, prostrations to the Guru, and a deep and steady resolve,
and having offered water for sipping (ācamana), gold, wine, and various fruits as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
One should cause the donor to bestow words of blessing for the attainment of his desired and perfect success.
Thus, for one whose heart is devoted, the worship of the true deity brings about a result equal to all [other merits]: the immediate fruit of the mind’s desire—
good fortune, long life, freedom from disease, an abundance of virtues, and the welfare of sentient beings.
Even through acts such as generosity, there exists the capacity to achieve perfection and attain great liberation.
May lions, water, fire, wind, elephants, night-stalkers, serpents, grief, calamities, disease, thieves, strife, obstacles, comets, and malevolent planets;
and may sin, poison, thunderbolts, sorcery, misfortune, and death— bring about peace.
Everything passes away before the rays of the sun, just as a mass of frost is dissolved by them.
To those whose wisdom is like the earth filled with various grains and gold; who possess mastery over sovereignty, fortune, armies, elephants, and horses, following in the footsteps of Indra;
and whose women are endowed with intellect, joy, beauty, youth, and the arts.
Like wealth scattered for the benefit of true friends, this is the nourishing [rite] for those whose nature is dharma.
Having been sprinkled with the Jvālāṅkana mantra and well-heated by Padmābha,
one should then dismiss [the deity] after making three snapping sounds and offering the *kṣānti* (forgiveness).
Having performed the worship of the feet of the assembly of maidens,
which was but a small measure of my skillful essence, it has long borne the drops of divine nectar.
May the person [attain this] from within the lotus-heart. || O ||
The exposition on the purpose of worshipping the maiden is completed. || 0 ||
